items.q: A pie is cut into 6 equal parts. You take 5 of the parts. What fraction of the pie did you take?
misconceptions: flipped the fraction upside down
counted one part instead of five
correct
counted the parts but forgot the whole
items.why: The pie was cut into 6 equal parts, so the bottom number is 6. You took 5 of them, so the top number is 5: 5/6.

items.q: A number line runs from 0 to 1 and is cut into 3 equal parts. Where does 2/3 sit?
misconceptions: went one mark too far, all the way to 1
placed it by feel: halfway is not a third mark
thought 2/3 is bigger than one whole
correct
items.why: Cutting 0 to 1 into 3 equal parts makes marks at 1/3, 2/3 and 1. Count 2 parts from 0 and you land on the second mark: 2/3.

items.q: In the fraction 3/6, what does the 6 tell you?
choices: The whole was cut into 6 equal parts
Each part is 6 times the whole
misconceptions: swapped the jobs of the top and bottom numbers
read the bottom number as a count of cakes
correct
made a part bigger than its whole
items.why: The bottom number says how many equal parts the whole was cut into. In 3/6 the whole was cut into 6 equal parts, and the 3 counts the parts you take.

items.q: Which fraction is the same as 1/3?
misconceptions: kept the top number and changed the share
picked a whole instead of a third
correct
changed the numbers without re-slicing evenly
items.why: Cut each third into 2 smaller pieces and both numbers double: 1/3 becomes 2/6. The pieces shrink, the count grows, and the share stays the same.

misconceptions: picked the fraction with bigger digits
checked the counts but not the piece sizes
gave up before using the halfway mark
correct
items.why: Use the halfway mark: half of 8 eighths is 4/8. 3/8 is less than 4/8, so 1/2 is greater.

items.q: Two cakes are the same size. Which serving is more: 2/3 of a cake or 2/4 of a cake?
misconceptions: thought a bigger bottom number means bigger pieces
matched the top numbers and stopped
correct
let the cutting order decide
items.why: Both servings are 2 pieces, but a cake cut into 3 has bigger pieces than one cut into 4. Two bigger pieces make more cake, so 2/3 is more.

misconceptions: added the bottom numbers too
dropped the piece size
added 2 sixths twice
correct
items.why: The pieces are the same size, sixths, so just count them: 2 sixths + 3 sixths = 5 sixths, or 5/6. The bottom number stays 6.

misconceptions: added the tops and the bottoms
added the tops but never re-sliced the half
correct
shrank both shares into tenths
items.why: The pieces do not match, so re-slice the half into eighths: 1/2 = 4/8. Then 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8.

items.q: Sam ate 1/3 of a pizza. Jo ate 1/6 of the same pizza. How much pizza did they eat in all?
misconceptions: added the tops and the bottoms
added the tops without re-slicing the third
multiplied the bottoms and guessed the top
correct
items.why: Re-slice the third into sixths: 1/3 = 2/6. Then 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6, and 3 sixths is half the pizza: 1/2.
